#9794. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. Hope you like this article if you have any question let me know in the comments section

#9793. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9792. When Blockchain Data Becomes AI Context, Stale State Becomes a Security Risk

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

Why autonomous agents need more than accurate retrieval when interacting with wallets, smart contracts, and decentralised protocols?

Blockchain systems are designed to maintain a shared record of transactions and state changes. AI agents are designed to interpret information, reason about goals, and decide what to do next. On paper, combining the two looks straightforward: give an agent access to blockchain data, let it understand the current situation, and allow it to act.

But there is a problem hidden inside that workflow. The data an AI agent retrieves can be correct when it is fetched, but still be unsafe to use when the agent acts on it.

A wallet balance may have changed. A transaction that appeared pending may have been confirmed. A decentralised exchange pool may have lost liquidity. A lending position may have moved closer to liquidation. An indexed view of a protocol may not yet reflect the latest block.

None of these situations necessarily requires a model to hallucinate. The agent can interpret every field correctly, follow its instructions, and produce a perfectly reasonable plan based on information that no longer describes the system it is about to interact with.

That is the kind of failure I find particularly important when thinking about production AI systems. We often concentrate on model quality, retrieval accuracy, and the amount of context an agent can process. Those things matter, but they do not answer a more fundamental question: Is the context still valid when the system uses it?

This becomes especially important in blockchain applications because an AI agent may move from reading information to initiating transactions. A stale answer in a chatbot can be corrected. A stale decision that results in a confirmed financial transaction may be much harder to recover from.

The challenge, then, is not simply to give AI agents more blockchain data. It is to design a system that understands where that data came from, which version of reality it represents, and whether it remains trustworthy enough to support the next action.

Consider a hypothetical AI agent responsible for monitoring a decentralised finance portfolio. The agent retrieves a wallet balance, checks a lending protocol, compares liquidity across two decentralised exchanges, and recommends moving a portion of the portfolio to a different position. Its calculations are correct. The relevant contract addresses are correct. The transaction it prepares respects the configured spending limit.

Yet the decision is still unsafe. Why? Because the information used to construct the transaction came from different moments in time.

The wallet balance was retrieved several seconds earlier. The exchange liquidity came from an indexer that was still processing recent events. The lending position was read from a separate RPC endpoint. Meanwhile, another transaction changed the wallet's balance, and the market moved.

Each response may have been valid when generated. Together, they no longer represent a consistent view of the system. This is a familiar category of distributed-systems problem: different components observe changes at different times. Blockchain infrastructure makes the problem particularly visible because applications often combine on-chain reads, event streams, indexed datasets, external price feeds, and local caches. An AI agent adds another stage to this process. It does not necessarily execute an action immediately after retrieving information. It may reason through several alternatives, call additional tools, summarise results, or ask another agent for an assessment. By the time the plan is ready, its original observations may already be outdated.

The important distinction is between data correctness at retrieval time and decision validity at execution time. These are not the same guarantee. A blockchain node can return the correct balance for the state it queried. An indexer can correctly process every event it has received. A retrieval system can return exactly the record requested. None of those facts guarantees that the complete context remains suitable for a transaction several seconds later. This is why I believe context engineering becomes much more than a retrieval problem when AI agents begin interacting with financial infrastructure. Context must be treated as a representation of system state, with explicit limits on how long that representation can be trusted.

One reason stale context is difficult to manage is that blockchain applications rarely obtain all their information from a single source.

These mechanisms serve different purposes. For example, Ethereum's JSON-RPC documentation distinguishes methods used to inspect state from methods used to retrieve historical information and track network activity. An application that combines these responses must understand what each response represents rather than treating every result as an interchangeable snapshot of reality.

Indexing adds another consideration. Services such as The Graph process blockchain events and expose structured data that applications can query more conveniently. This removes much of the burden of reconstructing useful application state from low-level blockchain data. However, an indexed representation is still a processed view of the chain. It depends on the progress of indexing, the logic used to interpret events, and the consistency of the underlying data pipeline.

A query returning successfully does not, by itself, establish that the indexer has caught up with the block relevant to the agent's decision. There is nothing inherently wrong with these architectures. Indexed data is valuable, RPC access is essential, and event-driven systems are often more efficient than repeatedly polling every contract.

The mistake is allowing the agent to interpret successful retrieval as proof of freshness. A context pipeline needs to communicate not just what a value is, but also where it came from, what state it describes, and what the application can safely infer from it.

The first response to stale context is often to add a timestamp or configure a time-to-live, commonly called a TTL. That is a useful starting point, but blockchain applications need a more careful approach.

Imagine an agent retrieves a token balance at 10:00:00 and prepares a transaction at 10:00:03. Three seconds may be perfectly acceptable for a low-risk monitoring task. The same delay may be unacceptable for an operation that depends on a rapidly changing exchange price or a lending position near a liquidation threshold. Now consider the opposite situation. An indexed record was produced a minute ago, but it represents a fully finalised block, and the application only needs historical reporting. That record may be entirely suitable for its purpose.

Age alone does not determine whether information is safe to use. Freshness depends on the decision, the source, the rate at which the relevant state can change, and the consequences of acting on an incorrect assumption. For blockchain-aware agents, I would distinguish at least four dimensions.

Temporal freshness: How much time has elapsed since the observation was made?

Chain freshness: Which block does the observation represent, and how does that block relate to the network's current state?

Source freshness: Has the relevant RPC endpoint or indexer processed the changes needed for this decision?

Decision freshness: Have the assumptions that justified the proposed action remained valid throughout planning and execution?

The fourth dimension is particularly important. An agent can retrieve fresh data, spend time reasoning about it, and then act on a plan whose assumptions have become invalid. A simple TTL cannot fully solve that problem. A more useful design assigns freshness requirements to the type of action. Reading historical transfers for a portfolio summary may require a different standard from submitting a swap or changing collateral in a lending protocol.

The system should be able to say not only, "This observation is three seconds old," but also, "This observation satisfies the requirements for this decision," or, "This information must be refreshed before execution." That is a much stronger foundation for reliable autonomy.

Blockchain applications have an additional advantage when managing freshness: they can associate observations with chain-specific identifiers.

On an Ethereum-compatible network, an application can record the block number and block hash associated with a state observation. This provides more useful information than a wall-clock timestamp alone. Suppose an agent reads a lending position and records that the observation came from block 24,000,100. It then retrieves market data and a wallet balance. If those observations refer to different blocks, the system knows that they may not represent the same chain state. That does not automatically make the observations unusable. Different block references may be perfectly acceptable for monitoring or exploratory analysis. But if the proposed action depends on a consistent set of values, the mismatch should be visible to the system. Block identifiers also matter because blockchain history is not always immediately final. Depending on the network and the observation being used, a block that was initially considered the head of the chain may later be replaced during a reorganisation.

Ethereum's JSON-RPC interface exposes block tags, including latest, safe, and finalized. These represent different positions in the chain's progression and offer ways to express what kind of state they need. The appropriate choice depends on the operation.

A monitoring agent may benefit from observing the latest available state to detect an emerging opportunity. A system recording a final accounting result may require a stronger finality guarantee. An agent preparing a transaction should understand which assumptions depend on provisional observations and which must hold before execution. There is no universal rule that every AI agent should wait for finalized state before doing anything. Waiting may introduce unnecessary latency for some applications. The engineering task is to make the trade-off explicit.

The system should know whether it is making a tentative observation, a decision based on a sufficiently stable state, or a conclusion that requires finalised data. Without that distinction, a model may treat every retrieved value as equally authoritative, even when the underlying blockchain guarantees are different.

Stale data is only part of the problem. An agent can also receive individually accurate observations that do not belong together. Consider a lending application. One tool returns the latest collateral value. Another returns a debt balance from an earlier block. A third retrieves a health factor calculated by an indexer that has not yet incorporated a recent repayment.

The model sees three plausible values and constructs a coherent explanation. But the explanation is based on a mixed snapshot. This is similar to a database transaction that reads different versions of related records without a suitable consistency strategy. Each record may be valid on its own, yet the combined view may never have existed as a single coherent state.

For an autonomous agent, that inconsistency can become an action. It might conclude that a position is safe when it is not. It might recommend a repayment amount that no longer matches the outstanding debt. It might prepare a transaction that exceeds the available balance after another operation has completed.

The solution is not necessarily to force every read through one expensive data source. Instead, the architecture should define which values must be consistent for a particular decision. For a transaction that depends on multiple pieces of contract state, the system might query the relevant values at a common block reference where supported. It might reject a plan if observations are too far apart, refresh the relevant contract state, or simulate the transaction against a sufficiently current state before submission. If a source cannot provide the required consistency guarantee, the agent should know that limitation.

This is an important principle for context engineering: relevance determines which information the agent needs; consistency determines whether that information can safely be used together. A context window can contain all the right facts and still describe a world that does not exist.

This problem becomes more interesting when an AI agent maintains memory across multiple steps or sessions. Memory is useful because an agent should not have to rediscover everything whenever a workflow resumes. It may need to remember that a user prefers a particular protocol, that a transaction failed previously, that an operation requires additional approval, or that a previous analysis identified a potential risk.

But not every fact deserves to remain authoritative indefinitely. Suppose an agent records the following observation: The wallet has sufficient USDC to execute the planned transaction.

That statement may have been correct when the agent recorded it. Later, another process transfers some of the funds. If the original statement remains in memory and is retrieved because it is semantically relevant, the agent may treat an outdated observation as a current balance. The retrieval system has not necessarily failed. It found exactly the information that matched the question. The problem is that the information's validity changed after it was stored.

This is one reason I distinguish between memory and state. Memory can preserve what the system observed, what it previously decided, why it made that decision, and what happened afterwards. An authoritative state must come from the appropriate source at the time the system needs to use it.

For blockchain applications, that distinction can be represented explicitly. A memory entry might say:

The last point is essential. A stored transaction identifier is useful evidence for finding an operation. There is no proof that the operation succeeded. The same rule applies to protocol eligibility, contract permissions, exchange liquidity, and previously approved transaction routes. A historical approval should not automatically become permanent authorisation for future transactions.

This does not mean an agent should discard its memory frequently. It means memory should preserve the distinction between historical facts, current observations, and assumptions that need revalidation. In practical terms, every piece of context that can become invalid should have a clear validity model. Some information may be valid until a policy changes. Other information may need to be refreshed before every financial action. Still, other information is historical and should never be presented as the current state.

The goal is not to make agents forget more. It is to prevent them from confusing what happened with what is happening now.

There is a further complication that is easy to overlook: even if every observation was fresh when retrieved, the plan built from those observations can become stale while the agent reasons. Imagine an agent evaluating three possible transaction routes. It gathers pool liquidity, estimates gas costs, calculates expected output, and compares the results. It then selects a route and prepares a transaction.

Between selection and submission, a relevant market condition changes. The agent may still have the original context in its prompt. Its reasoning may remain internally consistent. But the decision made is no longer supported by the same conditions.

I think this is where the design of agent runtimes becomes especially important. Context freshness cannot be handled only when information enters the model. It must also be considered at the boundary between planning and execution. A useful approach is to associate a decision with the observations and assumptions that justified it. For example, a proposed transaction could record:

The system can then determine whether the proposal remains valid before it is signed. This is more reliable than asking the model, "Are you still confident in this transaction?" Confidence is not a substitute for checking whether the relevant state has changed.

If a critical assumption no longer holds, the proposal should be invalidated. The agent can retrieve fresh data, recalculate the plan, and request another authorisation if required.

That makes the decision itself a managed object with a lifecycle, rather than a paragraph in the model's conversation history. It also helps separate two responsibilities that should not be confused: the model proposes an action, while the runtime determines whether the proposal is still valid for execution.

If I were designing a reference architecture for a blockchain-connected AI agent, I would avoid treating context as a single object assembled at the beginning of a workflow and passed unchanged through every subsequent step.

Instead, I would introduce a context validation layer between data retrieval, decision-making, and execution. The workflow would look something like this:

flowchart TDA["Blockchain RPC, Events, Indexers, Oracles"] --> B["Data Normalization and Provenance"]B --> C["Context Validation"]C -->|Valid for decision| D["AI Agent: Reason and Plan"]C -->|Stale or inconsistent| E["Refresh or Reject"]E --> BD --> F["Transaction Proposal"]F --> G["Execution-Time Validation"]G -->|Conditions satisfied| H["Policy Engine and Secure Signer"]G -->|Assumptions invalid| EH --> I["Blockchain Submission"]I --> J["Receipt and State Verification"]J --> K["Update Workflow State and Memory"]K --> C

The architecture does not require the model to understand every detail of blockchain consistency. It requires the surrounding system to expose enough metadata and enforce the appropriate rules. The data normalisation layer identifies the source and meaning of each observation. The context validation layer evaluates freshness and consistency according to the intended task. The agent uses validated information to propose a plan. The execution-time validator checks the assumptions that matter before a transaction can proceed.

Finally, the monitoring layer verifies what actually happened and updates the workflow state. This last step matters because a transaction being accepted by an RPC endpoint is not the same as a transaction being confirmed on-chain. A transaction receipt, its execution status, and the resulting state changes provide different evidence about the outcome.

If the submission response is lost or a timeout occurs, the system must not immediately assume failure and blindly submit the same operation again. It should inspect the known transaction identifier, check the relevant transaction state, and determine whether the original operation is pending, confirmed, replaced, or otherwise unresolved. Only then should it decide how to continue. This is where context engineering and distributed-systems engineering meet. The model needs useful context, but the runtime also needs a reliable record of what has been observed, what has been proposed, what has been authorised, and what has actually happened.

A practical system cannot refresh every value before every operation. That would increase latency, consume infrastructure capacity, and potentially make an otherwise useful agent too expensive to operate. The better approach is to align freshness requirements with the risk of the action. Consider three different tasks.

A portfolio reporting agent might summarise historical transfers and estimate the distribution of assets across wallets. It can often work with indexed data, provided that the report identifies the relevant block or time range and makes its limitations clear.

A monitoring agent might watch a lending position and notify the user when its health factor approaches a configured threshold. It needs sufficiently current information to make the alert useful, but it does not necessarily need permission to submit a transaction.

An autonomous transaction agent might adjust collateral or execute a swap. Its decision depends on the current state of relevant contracts, applicable permissions, and transaction-specific constraints. It needs stronger validation immediately before execution.

These tasks can use similar data sources while requiring different levels of assurance. This suggests that context freshness should be part of the application's policy model rather than a universal setting. The system might define a maximum observation age for a specific task, require a particular block reference, or demand that critical values be re-read immediately before signing. It could also specify when a task must stop and request human intervention.

The precise rules will differ across chains, protocols, and applications. The important thing is that they should be explicit, testable, and enforced outside the model. A useful operational principle is simple: the higher the impact of an incorrect action, the stronger the evidence required before that action is allowed.

Testing this problem requires more than checking whether an agent answers questions correctly. A system may perform well on static test data because the same balance, contract state, and market conditions remain unchanged throughout each test. Production environments are different. State changes while the agent is reasoning, external services become temporarily unavailable, and observations arrive in an unexpected order.

I would test the complete decision lifecycle, including the conditions under which the system refuses to act. For example, consider a test suite with the following scenarios.

Refresh the balance and recalculate the transaction

Detect the indexing lag or use an appropriate alternative source

Observations refer to incompatible block states

Reject or reconcile the context before a state-dependent decision

Invalidate affected observations and re-evaluate the decision

Resolve the transaction's status before retrying

Transaction simulation no longer matches current conditions

Stored memory contains an outdated approval

Revalidate the current policy and authorisation

The external data source becomes unavailable

Fail safely rather than silently treating old information as current

These tests should run under controlled conditions where the team can reproduce the same failure and inspect the system's behaviour. I would also measure more than task completion. Useful metrics include the age of critical observations when an action is authorised, the frequency of decisions rejected for stale state, the proportion of indexed observations that lag beyond their allowed threshold, and the number of transaction retries that occur without a verified execution status.

Another useful measure is the stale-action escape rate: how often an action based on an invalid or inconsistent state reaches the execution boundary instead of being rejected. For high-impact operations, the target should be zero unauthorised executions caused by known freshness violations. Achieving that requires testing the controls around the model, not merely improving its ability to recognise outdated information in a prompt.

There is also a cost to consider. Refreshing every observation, querying multiple providers, and repeatedly simulating transactions can increase latency and infrastructure consumption. The engineering objective is to establish the minimum evidence required for each action without adding unnecessary checks to low-risk tasks. A good evaluation should therefore measure both safety and operational efficiency.

When an AI agent makes an incorrect decision, a log entry saying that a tool call succeeded is rarely enough to diagnose the failure. Suppose an agent executes a transaction based on a balance that had changed several seconds earlier. The transaction succeeds technically, but the resulting position violates the user's intended allocation.

To understand what happened, the team needs to reconstruct the decision. Which balance did the agent observe? Which block did it refer to? What did the indexer report? How old was the price data? Which assumptions did the plan depend on? Was the transaction simulated? Did the policy engine validate the proposal against the fresh state? What did the blockchain ultimately confirm?

Without this information, engineers may blame the model when the real failure occurred in the data pipeline or execution layer. I would treat decision observability as a first-class part of the architecture. For every consequential action, the system should maintain a trace linking the observations used, their provenance, the proposed transaction, the applicable policy checks, the authorisation result, and the confirmed outcome.

Sensitive information, particularly private keys and credentials, must never be exposed in these records. The objective is to preserve enough structured evidence to reconstruct the decision without creating another security vulnerability. This is also where context versioning becomes valuable. If a team can establish exactly which observations and policy versions supported a decision, it can reproduce the relevant conditions in a test environment and determine which safeguard failed.

Observability should answer a more useful question than "Did the agent call the tool?" It should answer: "Was the action justified by the information available, and did that information remain valid when the system authorised execution?"

One of the appealing properties of blockchain is that transaction history can be independently verified. But that property can create a misleading sense of security when applications consume blockchain information through multiple layers of infrastructure.

A verifiable ledger does not automatically make every API response current. A correctly indexed event does not guarantee that an application has processed every subsequent event. A valid price-feed response does not establish that its value is appropriate for every financial decision. Trust must be considered across the complete path from the underlying state to the action taken by the agent. That means understanding the guarantees offered by each component, monitoring where those guarantees can weaken, and refusing to let a successful response stand in for a stronger guarantee that the source never provided. The same principle applies to AI memory. A model may recall an observation accurately without knowing that the observation has expired. A retrieval system may rank an outdated record highly because it is relevant to the current query. A reasoning model may then produce a convincing plan that is no longer safe to execute. The answer is not to ask the model to be more careful. It is to give the surrounding system the information and authority needed to enforce the distinction between historical knowledge and the current state.

As AI agents move toward financial and operational applications, the conversation around context needs to change. We have become accustomed to asking whether a model has enough information, whether retrieval is accurate, and whether its context window is large enough. Those questions remain important, but they are incomplete when the model can initiate actions in an external system. For blockchain-connected agents, a more useful set of questions is:

These are not merely questions about prompt construction. There are questions about data integrity, state management, authorisation, and distributed execution. I see this as an important direction for production AI engineering. As agents become more capable, the surrounding infrastructure must become better at distinguishing information that is useful from information that is safe to act upon. Blockchain makes that distinction particularly consequential because the agent's decisions may result in financial transactions that cannot simply be undone.

The objective should not be to eliminate every delay or force every workflow to wait for the strongest possible confirmation. Different applications have different requirements, and latency, cost, and safety will always need to be balanced. The objective is to make those trade-offs explicit, measurable, and enforceable. An AI agent should know when its information is sufficient to proceed, when its assumptions need to be refreshed, and when uncertainty is too high to justify an action. The real challenge is not teaching an AI agent to understand blockchain data. It is building a system that knows when that understanding is no longer safe to trust. That is where context engineering becomes an essential part of blockchain security, and where reliable autonomous systems will have to prove themselves.

Human approval is not a security boundary unless it is bound to the exact action being approved, enf

#9791. Identity is the new firewall : avec les CVE et l’IA, il est temps de remettre des barrières

Nous enchaînons les CVE à un rythme qui pose une véritable question d’architecture. Peut-on encore considérer qu’une application exposée sur Internet restera suffisamment sécurisée pour lui confier seule la protection de ses accès ? Nous multiplions les applications, leurs dépendances, leurs frameworks et leurs cycles de mises à jour, tout en sachant qu’une seule vulnérabilité peut suffire à compromettre un système.

Prenons Confluence. En 2023, la CVE-2023-22515 permettait à un attaquant non authentifié de créer un compte administrateur sur certaines versions. En 2024, la CVE-2024-27198 de TeamCity permettait de contourner son authentification et potentiellement de compromettre entièrement le serveur. Ces vulnérabilités concernaient des applications professionnelles largement déployées, maintenues par des éditeurs reconnus, dont les mécanismes de sécurité étaient pourtant contournables.

Avec l'IA, cette situation devient encore moins confortable. L'analyse de vulnérabilités, la recherche de chemins d'exploitation et l'automatisation des attaques peuvent s'accélérer. Nous ne pouvons plus construire notre sécurité en pariant sur la capacité de chaque éditeur à corriger ses applications avant qu'un attaquant ne les exploite. Notre architecture doit rester défendable même lorsqu'une application est vulnérable.

Chez Ariovis, nous avons fait un choix que je trouve de plus en plus pertinent : remonter une partie de la sécurité au niveau des middlewares et de l'infrastructure, avant même que les requêtes n'atteignent nos applications.

En plaçant un reverse proxy Nginx devant nos outils, avec une authentification fédérée en OpenID Connect (OIDC), nous imposons un contrôle d'identité indépendant du logiciel protégé. L'utilisateur doit s'authentifier auprès de notre fournisseur d'identité avant que le proxy n'autorise sa requête. L'application conserve ses propres contrôles, mais elle ne constitue plus notre unique ligne de défense.

Reprenons TeamCity. Si son mécanisme d'authentification peut être contourné par une CVE, un reverse proxy correctement configuré continuera d'exiger une identité valide avant de laisser passer la requête malveillante. La vulnérabilité applicative existe toujours, mais son exploitation anonyme depuis Internet devient beaucoup plus difficile. Nous avons déplacé la frontière de sécurité hors du composant qui présente la faille.

Je considère aussi qu'il est plus raisonnable de maîtriser un nombre limité de composants d'authentification standardisés que de dépendre de dizaines d'implémentations applicatives différentes. Nginx n'est pas invulnérable, et aucune statistique ne permet d'affirmer qu'il sera toujours moins vulnérable que les applications protégées. En revanche, cette architecture réduit le nombre de mécanismes d'authentification à maintenir et nous permet d'intervenir directement sur la politique d'accès, sans dépendre du calendrier de chaque éditeur.

Encore faut-il que toutes les routes sensibles passent réellement par ce contrôle et que les serveurs applicatifs ne soient pas directement joignables. C'est une contrainte d'architecture que nous pouvons maîtriser et vérifier.

L'autre réaction face à l'augmentation des vulnérabilités consiste à tout refermer. Héberger ses applications en cloud privé, supprimer leurs expositions publiques et contrôler strictement les flux réseau est une stratégie parfaitement défendable. Mais elle peut devenir pénible pour les utilisateurs, surtout lorsqu'elle repose sur des VPN traditionnels donnant accès à des portions entières du système d'information.

Chez Ariovis, nous combinons cette isolation avec du ZTNA et des contrôles d'identité au niveau des reverse proxies. Nos ressources internes ne sont pas directement accessibles depuis Internet ; l'accès réseau est conditionné à l'identité, tandis que le middleware contrôle les requêtes HTTP avant leur transmission aux applications.

Cette combinaison renverse notre manière de penser le pare-feu. Le réseau est verrouillé par défaut, mais c'est l'identité qui permet de le déverrouiller pour atteindre une ressource précise. Le collaborateur accède à ses outils grâce à son identité, sans devoir nécessairement connaître leur emplacement réseau ou gérer un VPN complexe.

Le SSO apporte ici un bénéfice supplémentaire : l'authentification forte, les politiques d'accès conditionnel et la révocation des sessions sont centralisées. Nous pouvons modifier les conditions d'entrée de plusieurs applications sans intervenir dans chacune de leurs bases de code. C'est aussi une manière de réduire les délais de réaction lorsqu'une application devient particulièrement exposée.

Les agents IA vont multiplier les interactions entre applications, API et données. Chaque nouvel outil connecté à un agent représente potentiellement un nouveau chemin d'accès, tandis que les identités non humaines et les délégations introduisent des risques que le SSO traditionnel ne couvre pas entièrement.

La réponse ne consiste pas à permettre à un agent authentifié de tout faire. Nous devons distinguer trois contrôles : l'identité qui autorise l'ouverture du chemin réseau, l'authentification qui permet d'atteindre le service et l'autorisation qui détermine ce que l'agent peut effectivement exécuter. Pour les appels machine-à-machine, des jetons OAuth adaptés et des contrôles d'autorisation au niveau des API complètent les protections destinées aux utilisateurs humains.

Cette séparation est essentielle : une authentification réussie ne garantit jamais qu'une action soit légitime. Elle permet néanmoins de conserver une première frontière de sécurité indépendante de la logique applicative, y compris lorsque celle-ci évolue rapidement.

Nous appliquons cette approche à notre propre système d'information, avec une infrastructure hybride, des ressources protégées derrière un reverse proxy fédéré à Microsoft Entra ID et des mécanismes d'accès réseau conditionnel.

Ariovis a obtenu sa certification ISO/IEC 27001:2022 le 25 octobre 2026. Notre audit de certification de deuxième étape n'a relevé aucune non-conformité, majeure ou mineure. Ce résultat ne signifie pas que nos applications seront exemptes de vulnérabilités, mais il confirme la conformité du système de management audité, dont les contrôles d'accès font partie.

« Identity is the new firewall » était une conviction d'architecte IAM. Aujourd'hui, c'est une réponse concrète à la multiplication des vulnérabilités applicatives et à l'accélération des usages de l'IA.

Nous ne pouvons pas garantir que toutes nos applications resteront sécurisées. Nous pouvons en revanche décider qu'aucune application interne ne sera seule responsable de sa propre protection.

#9790. Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard

A few months ago, we added private data to the Open ASR Leaderboard: 11 splits from Appen and DataOceanAI covering scripted and conversational speech from five accents (blog). The community response was great, with many highlighting the importance of held-out sets for trustworthy evaluations. Since then, we added one more private split for Indian-accented English with Voice Arena (blog).

We’re excited to announce a new collaboration with Liva AI to add even more private data with two new accents: Egyptian 🇪🇬 and Nigerian 🇳🇬.

This is part of our continued effort to improve representation in ASR evals (more accents and more languages) and to improve trust (new private data to minimize benchmaxxing, and new data providers). We’re excited to see the community continuing to push ASR performance for the world 🤗

With these new accents, we can now present a richer breakdown of accents, based on Kachru’s Three Circles (kudos to Hume AI for this idea in their leaderboard). The Open ASR Leaderboard will now report:

As more accents join, we’ll split the Outer and Expanding Circles.

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.

#9789. Where an e-commerce explainer video belongs, and what to show in it

Most online shops add a video the same way they add a banner: somewhere on the home page, because that is where the space is. The video then gets a few views, no one measures it, and the team decides video "doesn't work". The problem is usually placement and content, not the medium. Here is how I decide both when a store asks me to animate something.

A shopper does not need a video everywhere. They need it at the exact point where they hesitate. In a store that is usually one of three places.

The product page of a product that is hard to judge from photos. Anything with a mechanism, a size relationship or a setup step: a 20-second clip showing it in use answers questions the photo gallery cannot. This is the highest-value spot, and it is the one most stores skip.

The cart or checkout step, for a policy that causes drop-off. If shoppers abandon because they are unsure about returns, delivery windows or subscription cancellation, a short plain explanation beside that step does more than a longer FAQ page.

The first ad touch. For paid social, the video is the ad. Here the rules are different: the first two seconds must carry the point, and it must work with the sound off.

The home page hero is the last place I would start. Visitors there have not decided what they care about yet, so the video has nothing specific to answer.

Whatever the placement, the structure that holds up is short:

Cut anything that does not serve one of those four. Most first drafts are twice as long as they need to be.

For a product page, 15 to 30 seconds is plenty. For a policy or how-it-works clip, up to 45. For ads, render a 9:16 and a 1:1 from the same project so you do not rebuild it for each platform. Always add captions, since a large share of shoppers watch muted.

Pick the single number the video is supposed to move before it ships: add-to-cart rate on that product, checkout completion, or click-through on the ad. Compare the pages with and without it for a couple of weeks. If it does not move that number, fix the placement or the opening seconds before blaming the format.

I wrote a longer version of this, with examples by product type, here: https://vaghelabhavesh.com/blog/ecommerce-explainer-video-guide.html

#9788. ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

#9787. A 100% coverage threshold that CI never ran

The core package in Styx has a 100% coverage threshold in its config. It turned out CI never ran coverage, so nothing enforced the number. The selector tests had quietly fallen short.

The fix came in as a pull request. It added tests for the selector behaviour that was missing, and added one command to the CI matrix: pnpm -F @styx/core exec vitest run --coverage. After it, 664 tests pass with 1390 of 1390 statements and 1102 of 1102 branches covered.

The part I like is what it did with the branches it couldn't cover. A few fallbacks were unreachable, so it simplified them away instead of writing contrived tests for them. The observable results stayed the same, and the code got smaller.

Two lessons. A threshold in a config file is a wish until the command that enforces it runs in CI. And when the last few percent won't go green, ask whether that code can run at all.

I only ask for 100% on the pure packages, the state machines, policy and selectors, where it's cheap. I wouldn't ask it of UI code.
