#9786. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9785. A Nasty Sign Of Omega-3 Deficiency

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

Stiffness in the joints and swelling can be indirect signs of omega-3 deficiency, research suggests.

Waking up stiff in the morning, feeling pain in the joints, swelling, tenderness and loss of flexibility are all signs of arthritis.

Omega-3 deficiency could be contributing, as scientists believe there is a link between this leading cause of disability and a lack of omega-3 in the diet.

Researchers suggest that a diet rich in omega-3 could decrease the symptoms of osteoarthritis.

A study has found that adding fish oil to the diet — and to some degree flaxseed oil (alpha-linolenic acid has an anti-inflammatory effect) — can ease or even prevent osteoarthritis.

With population aging, osteoarthritis will be one of the leading causes of disability.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, by 2040 it is estimated that 26% of US adults aged 18 or older will be diagnosed by a doctor with arthritis.

While there are still no effective medications for treating this condition, omega-3 fish oil can be one of the best natural remedies in treating osteoarthritis.

Professor John Tarlton, the lead researcher of the study, explained the effect of omega-3 on osteoarthritis:

“Classic early signs of the condition, such as the degradation of collagen in cartilage and the loss of molecules that give it shock-absorbing properties, were both reduced with omega-3.

Furthermore, there was strong evidence that omega-3 influences the biochemistry of the disease, and therefore not only helps prevent disease, but also slows its progression, potentially controlling established osteoarthritis.”

Western diets contain high levels of omega-6 fatty acids, which can lead to inflammatory disorders such as colitis, heart disease, osteoporosis, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis.

Modern diets contain up to 30 times more omega-6 than omega-3, whereas our ancestor’s diets contained almost an equal level of these two omega fatty acids.

Therefore, supplementation with omega-3 can help to restore this imbalance in Western diets and improve conditions such as colitis and heart-related diseases.

Fish oil is much more effective than flax seed oil, but for vegetarians and vegans this supplement is an important option.

“Most diets in the developed world are lacking in omega-3, with modern diets having up to 30 times too much omega-6 and too little omega-3.

Taking omega-3 will help redress this imbalance and may positively contribute to a range of other health problems such as heart disease and colitis.”

The study was published in the journal of Osteoarthritis and Cartilage (Knott et al., 2011).

#9784. Decentralized AI Inference Needs a Boring Job Queue

Self-taught backend engineer from Nigeria. I build APIs and job queues with TypeScript and Node.js, and run a dev agency for Nigerian SMEs.

Self-taught backend engineer from Nigeria. I build APIs and job queues with TypeScript and Node.js, and run a dev agency for Nigerian SMEs.

Self-taught backend engineer from Nigeria. I build APIs and job queues with TypeScript and Node.js, and run a dev agency for Nigerian SMEs.

Whenever people talk about decentralized AI, the conversation usually revolves around GPUs, tokens, and governance.

But there's another problem that doesn't get nearly as much attention.

How do you get an AI request from an application to a remote GPU and back without things falling apart along the way?

Imagine sending a request to a GPU on a decentralized network. The GPU finishes the job, but the worker responsible for saving the result crashes.

Now you're left wondering: Did the GPU finish the job? Should I try again? And if I do, will I end up paying twice for the same work?

These might sound like small problems, but anyone who has worked with backend systems knows how messy things can get when different services depend on one another.

I'm a backend engineer, and I work with things like APIs, job queues, retries, and idempotency. So when I look at decentralized AI, I don't just think about how to access GPUs. I also think about what happens when things go wrong.

This article is my proposal for making decentralized GPU inference feel more like a regular backend service that developers can actually rely on.

I'm a self-taught backend engineer from Nigeria. I work with TypeScript, Node.js, MongoDB, Redis, RabbitMQ, BullMQ, and Docker. I also build web and mobile products for Nigerian SMEs.

One thing that makes AI infrastructure interesting to me is the cost.

GPU compute is often priced in dollars, while many of the businesses around me earn in naira. As a product grows and starts making more AI requests, those costs can become harder to manage.

Depending entirely on one provider also comes with risks. Prices can change, services can become unavailable, and your application can become too dependent on a single company.

Decentralized GPU networks offer another option by connecting users with computing resources operated by different providers.

That's promising, but getting access to a GPU is only part of the story.

Developers still need a reliable way to send jobs, recover from failures, retrieve results, and keep track of what they're paying for.

Let's say you're building an application that uses AI.

A user submits a request, and your backend sends it to a remote GPU to process.

You also have to think about duplicate requests and billing. If your system retries a job after a timeout, how do you know the original job isn't still running?

These aren't problems unique to decentralized AI. They're challenges developers already face when building systems that depend on multiple services.

Thankfully, we already have tools that can help.

Job queues, databases, retries, and idempotency are all useful building blocks. They won't magically prevent every failure, but they can help us handle failures in a more controlled way.

I'd build the system around four main components.

The first component would be a simple API built with Express.js and TypeScript.

Its job would be to receive the request, check that it's valid, authenticate the user, and create a record for the job.

Instead of making the user wait for the entire AI computation to finish, the API would return a job ID immediately.

For example, a client could send a request to:

The user could then check the job's status or retrieve the result later.

The important thing is that the application wouldn't need to know which specific GPU provider is handling the request.

Next, I'd use BullMQ and Redis to manage background jobs, with PostgreSQL keeping the authoritative record of each job.

Think of the queue as a system that organizes work and makes sure it gets picked up for processing.

Each job would contain the information needed to execute it, including the model, input, deadline, retry limit, idempotency key, and billing details.

If something goes wrong, it could move to failed or into a reconciliation state while the system figures out what happened.

That second option matters more than it might seem.

A timeout doesn't always mean the job failed. Sometimes the GPU has already finished the work, but your backend lost contact with it before saving the result.

If you immediately submit the job again, you could end up paying for another execution unnecessarily.

Redis and BullMQ would help coordinate the work, while PostgreSQL would preserve the job's history and status even if a worker or service restarts.

The third component would connect the backend to the actual GPU network.

I'd start with one provider, such as Nosana, rather than trying to support every decentralized compute network from day one.

A worker would take a job from the queue, prepare it for the provider, submit it, and track its progress.

I'd also create a small adapter that gives the rest of the application a consistent way to interact with the provider.

Conceptually, it would support three operations:

The idea is simple: the application shouldn't have to deal with every provider's unique API and status codes.

The adapter would handle those differences and translate them into a format the backend understands.

Once the first integration works, I could look at adding other providers, self-hosted GPUs, or even centralized AI services.

But first, I'd make one integration work properly.

Getting a response from a GPU doesn't automatically mean the job is successful.

The backend still needs to check the result before marking the job as complete.

For a text-generation request, that could mean checking:

Large results could be saved in object storage, while PostgreSQL keeps the metadata, content hash, storage location, and execution details.

I could explore something like Arweave later if there's a real need for permanent, independently accessible storage.

But there's an important distinction here: a content hash can help show that a file hasn't changed. It doesn't prove that the GPU generated the correct answer.

For the first version, I'd focus on handling jobs and results correctly before adding more infrastructure.

Here's how I'd expect a request to move through the system:

Of course, things won't always go this smoothly.

A worker could crash, a provider could become unreachable, or a result could arrive when the backend isn't ready to save it.

That's why retries and recovery need to be part of the design from the beginning, rather than something added after the first failure.

This is where I'd spend a lot of my attention.

Every job would have a deadline, and each provider execution would have its own ID.

If a worker loses contact with a provider, the system should first try to find out what happened.

Is the job still running? Did it finish? Did it fail?

If the provider offers a way to check execution status, the worker can use that information to decide what to do next.

If the result is still available, the backend could retrieve it instead of running the job again.

But what if the system can't determine the outcome?

In that case, it should record the uncertainty instead of blindly submitting another paid execution.

Sometimes the system won't have enough information to make a safe decision. I'd rather make that limitation visible than pretend every failure can be resolved automatically.

Imagine a user submits an AI request, but their internet connection drops before the API responds.

Without the right safeguards, the backend might create two separate jobs.

The API would accept an idempotency key and use a database uniqueness constraint to ensure that repeated submissions with the same key return the existing logical job instead of creating another one.

I'd also give billing records their own duplicate protection and store each provider execution separately.

That way, the system can distinguish between one logical job and the different execution attempts associated with it.

However, there's a limitation worth being honest about.

Preventing duplicate jobs in my backend doesn't guarantee that the GPU provider will execute the work only once.

If a provider doesn't support safe repeated submissions or reliable status checks, the backend may not know whether an interrupted request was actually processed.

At that point, the system might need manual intervention or a decision about whether to risk another execution.

That's not a problem I'd hide behind a promise of "exactly-once execution." I'd document it and work within what the provider can actually guarantee.

Some jobs will fail repeatedly, even after retries.

Instead of retrying forever, I'd move them into a failure-handling workflow once they've exhausted their retry budget.

The system would preserve the error messages, execution history, and provider details so someone could investigate what happened.

An operator should be able to understand why a job failed and decide whether it's safe to try again.

Jobs shouldn't disappear silently, but retrying them endlessly isn't the answer either.

This is another area that needs careful thought.

One possible approach is to run the same inference on two different nodes and compare their outputs.

That can be useful for deterministic workloads under controlled conditions.

But generative AI doesn't always return identical outputs for the same input. Sampling settings, execution environments, and implementation differences can all affect the result.

So if two nodes return different outputs, that alone doesn't prove that either one is dishonest.

I'd begin with basic validation and controlled test workloads where the expected behavior is easier to check.

Later, I could explore spot checks, redundant execution, and more advanced methods for verifying inference.

There's a trade-off, though. Running a job multiple times means paying for additional compute.

The extra verification should be worth the cost.

I'd also keep job status and payment status separate.

A job might finish successfully while its payment is still pending. Likewise, a payment-related operation could fail even though the GPU completed the work.

The system should record estimated costs, provider-reported execution outcomes, and billing status independently.

If the provider supports an appropriate payment or escrow mechanism, I could integrate it later.

But I wouldn't promise escrow protection without confirming that the underlying provider can actually support it.

I don't think decentralization is valuable simply because it's decentralized.

What interests me is the possibility of giving developers more flexibility and reducing their dependence on a single provider.

But that only becomes useful if integrating decentralized compute isn't a headache.

A developer should be able to submit an inference request, receive a job ID, check its status, and retrieve the result through a consistent interface.

They shouldn't have to rewrite their entire application every time they change GPU providers.

For example, a request might go to a decentralized GPU network, a self-hosted GPU, or a centralized AI API.

The adapter would make common operations easier, while clearly identifying the differences that matter.

That's the goal: reduce unnecessary complexity without pretending every provider is the same.

This is still a proposal. I haven't benchmarked a working implementation, so I don't have results to claim yet.

I'd submit the same inference request repeatedly using the same idempotency key.

Then I'd check whether the API returns the same logical job, whether duplicate queue messages are handled safely, and whether the billing records remain unique.

I'd simulate a worker crashing after the provider accepts a job but before the result is saved.

The question is whether the system can recover the existing execution, retrieve the result, or identify an uncertain outcome without automatically launching another paid job.

I'd compare sending a request directly to the provider with sending it through the gateway and queue.

I'd measure the extra latency, total completion time, success and failure rates, and how many provider executions were needed per logical job.

I'd also document the model, hardware or provider configuration, sample size, and testing conditions.

That way, anyone reading the results could understand what was tested and how meaningful the numbers are.

With access to suitable Nosana credits, I'd start with:

I'd leave multi-provider routing, permanent decentralized storage, on-chain escrow, and advanced inference verification for later.

There's no point building ten extra features before proving that the basic system works.

The first milestone is simple: send a request from an application to a remote GPU, get the result back, and show what happens when something goes wrong.

Decentralized AI needs more than GPUs and a good token model.

It also needs the backend infrastructure that makes remote computation usable in real applications.

That means keeping track of jobs, handling retries carefully, recovering from failures, checking results, and making billing understandable.

Fortunately, we don't have to invent every building block from scratch. Many of these tools already exist.

The real challenge is putting them together in a way that accounts for the uncertainties of working with independently operated compute providers.

I'm approaching this as a backend engineer who's interested in solving a practical problem, not someone claiming to have already figured everything out.

My next step is to build a small working version, test the failure cases, and share what the measurements actually show.

If you're building in decentralized compute, I'd love to hear how you're handling execution recovery, result verification, and duplicate billing.

Those are the problems I want to understand better.

Self-taught backend engineer from Nigeria. I build APIs and job queues with TypeScript and Node.js, and run a dev agency for Nigerian SMEs.

#9783. ¿Por qué git checkout no puede deshacer lo que cambió un agente de IA en tu código?

Cuando un agente de IA edita archivos de tu proyecto y rompe algo, el reflejo es git checkout -- . o git stash. Los dos responden a una pregunta distinta de la que tienes. Git puede llevarte al último commit. Lo que quieres es la carpeta tal como estaba justo antes del turno del agente, con tu propio trabajo sin commitear y los archivos que git ignora, y sin los archivos que creó el agente.

La aplicación de escritorio de osFoundry lo resuelve con un pequeño almacén direccionado por contenido escrito en Rust, checkpoint_store.rs. Antes de que una escritura del agente llegue a un archivo, los bytes actuales del archivo se guardan en /.osfoundry/checkpoints/blobs/, y /rewind los vuelve a escribir. Aquí tienes el mismo diseño en unas 90 líneas de Python con solo la biblioteca estándar, comparado con cuatro recetas de git sobre un turno realista y cronometrado sobre una copia de un árbol de código TypeScript real de 4,686 archivos.

El proyecto de prueba es un sitio diminuto en un repositorio git: index.html, styles.css (212 líneas), app.js y un .env que .gitignore excluye. Después del último commit, el usuario cambió el título de la página en index.html y empezó un notes.md sin seguimiento. Ese es el estado al que hay que volver.

Luego viene el turno del agente: reescribe styles.css hasta dejarlo en 41 líneas, edita index.html para cargar un nuevo theme.css, reescribe app.js, apunta API_URL en .env a localhost y crea theme.css. Cada método de deshacer se ejecutó sobre una copia limpia, y un script comparó cada archivo byte a byte con el estado anterior al turno.

Los resultados de git se deducen de lo que es git. Restaura el último commit, o una instantánea de los archivos con seguimiento y en staging, y ambas cosas mezclan tu trabajo con el del agente en cuanto ninguno de los dos está commiteado. Los archivos ignorados le resultan invisibles salvo que añadas -a, y un checkout nunca borra un archivo que no existía en la instantánea. La última fila es la configuración de git más justa, una instantánea tomada antes de cada turno, y aun así falla en dos de los cinco archivos. Además tiene un efecto secundario: git add -A pone en staging todo tu trabajo en el índice real en cada turno.

Un checkpoint es una lista por turno: para cada archivo que escribió el agente, o bien el hash de su contenido anterior, o bien una nota de que no existía. Los bytes van a blobs/ una sola vez por cada contenido distinto.

Tres detalles deciden si una restauración es correcta, y cada uno es también una regla en el módulo de Rust.

Gana la primera captura de una ruta en un turno. Un agente escribe a menudo el mismo archivo varias veces en un turno. Rebobinar significa volver a cómo estaba el archivo cuando empezó el turno, no a algún estado entre dos escrituras del propio agente, así que las capturas posteriores de la misma ruta en el mismo turno se ignoran.

Un archivo que no existe se registra como absent. Esa única línea es lo que permite que una restauración borre theme.css. Git no tiene equivalente para "este archivo no debe existir", salvo un git clean que también borra archivos que querías conservar.

Los archivos de más de 8 MB se registran como skipped con un motivo, no se omiten. Así, una restauración informa de que no pudo devolverlos, en lugar de terminar en silencio con una mezcla de archivos viejos y nuevos.

Rebobinar el turno 1 cuando después vinieron los turnos 2 y 3 debe deshacer los tres. Restaurar solo el turno 1 dejaría archivos del turno 2 junto a archivos de antes del turno 1, una combinación que nunca existió. El orden también importa. Para un archivo tocado en varios turnos, los bytes correctos son la preimagen más antigua, la que se capturó cuando empezó el turno 1. Recorrer del más reciente al más antiguo acaba en la preimagen del turno 2, que es el estado que produjo el turno 1. El código Rust tiene un comentario justo sobre esto: al principio se escribió del más reciente al más antiguo, y el test rewinding_a_turn_also_undoes_later_turns lo detectó.

La comprobación de la ruta se repite al restaurar porque index.json es un archivo normal dentro de la carpeta que describe. Si se confiara en él, cualquiera o cualquier cosa capaz de editarlo podría hacer que una restauración escribiera en cualquier parte del disco. Después, los turnos rebobinados se eliminan del índice, para que un segundo rebobinado al mismo punto no pueda "tener éxito" sobre archivos que ya están de vuelta.

El árbol es una copia de la carpeta src de una app real de React y TypeScript: 4,686 archivos, 121.4 MB, ninguno de más de 8 MB. En cada turno se eligieron archivos al azar, se capturaron y se les añadió una línea; luego se ejecutó una restauración y se comparó cada archivo con el original. Todas las restauraciones coincidieron. Apple M1, 8 GB, macOS 15, SSD con APFS, Python 3.9.6, git 2.39.5.

Para comparar, la instantánea de git por turno del escenario anterior (git add -A y luego git stash create) tardó entre 61 y 68 ms en este árbol sin ningún cambio, y entre 50 y 67 ms con cuatro archivos editados. Tiene que mirar los 4,686 archivos cada vez. Justo después de la ejecución que reescribió todos los archivos, la siguiente tardó 1,241 ms, porque git vuelve a calcular el hash de cada archivo cuya marca de tiempo cambió. Un checkpoint solo mira los archivos que se están escribiendo, así que un turno normal cuesta unos pocos milisegundos sea cual sea el tamaño del proyecto.

La última fila deja ver un problema en el código tal como está. La captura media tardó 1.29 ms en los primeros 100 archivos del turno y 9.54 ms en los últimos 100. Cada captura reescribe el index.json entero, que llegó a 1.3 MB, así que el coste de cada escritura crece con el número de escrituras anteriores. Sustituir _save por un append de una línea JSON por captura lo arregló con los mismos 4,686 archivos: 2.5 s en total, 0.41 ms por captura al principio y 0.61 ms al final. Para un agente que edita unos pocos archivos por turno, la versión simple basta. Para un formateador o un renombrado en todo el código ejecutado a través de un agente, usa el log de solo append.

Nombrar los blobs por su SHA-256 deduplica los bytes idénticos y nada más. Tres mediciones muestran dónde queda eso.

En todo el árbol, 4,686 archivos tenían 4,677 contenidos distintos, así que un turno sobre el árbol completo guardó 4,677 blobs. Los archivos duplicados son raros en un árbol de código real.

Un archivo de 2 MB reescrito en diez turnos, con el agente añadiendo una línea cada vez: diez preimágenes, todas distintas, 10 blobs y 20.0 MB. El mismo archivo, pero el agente escribe los mismos bytes en cada turno, como hace un reintento que produce una salida idéntica: 2 blobs y 4.0 MB, el original y la versión desde la que partió cada turno posterior. En los dos casos, rebobinar al primer turno devolvió el original byte a byte.

Los blobs se guardan sin comprimir. Los 121.4 MB de blobs del turno sobre el árbol completo serían 33.7 MB con zlib a nivel 6, y el propio almacén de objetos de git para el mismo árbol tras un commit ocupaba 41.0 MB. La compresión es un añadido razonable si el almacén se conserva mucho tiempo, ya que el código fuente se comprime aproximadamente 3.6 a 1. Los deltas entre versiones, como en los pack files de git, ahorrarían más en el caso de añadir una línea, pero cuestan mucho más código del que necesita un almacén de preimágenes.

Solo ve las escrituras que pasan por write(). Si tu agente también puede ejecutar comandos de shell, un rm o un sed -i se le escapan por completo. La aplicación de osFoundry hace pasar las escrituras de archivos del agente por una sola función, que es donde captura.

Una restauración escribe la preimagen sin importar lo que haya ahora en el archivo. Si editaste un archivo a mano después del agente, rebobinar ese turno también reemplaza tu edición. Una versión más estricta registra el hash de lo que escribió el agente y, antes de restaurar, comprueba si el archivo sigue teniendo ese hash. Si no, guarda primero los bytes actuales como un blob más, de modo que también se pueda deshacer la restauración.

Además, el almacén crece hasta que se rebobinan turnos. Basta con un prune que borre los blobs a los que no hace referencia ningún checkpoint, más un límite de cuántos turnos conservar.

Los dos bloques de la clase de arriba son el almacén completo, Python 3.9 con la biblioteca estándar y nada que instalar. La aplicación de escritorio de osFoundry incluye la versión en Rust como /rewind en los chats que trabajan en una carpeta local, gratis desde la página de descarga de osFoundry.

#9782. Desktops have SQLite. Servers have Postgres. Now, the browser finally has WebDB — Introducing WebDB

Stop shipping multi-megabyte desktop databases to the browser—the Web finally has its own DB.

If you’ve ever built an offline-first or local-first web application, you already know the storage struggle. Everything starts out fine when you're just caching a few JSON objects. Then, real product requirements kick in: you need to join orders with customers, filter by multiple conditions, calculate totals, paginate results, and keep two open browser tabs in sync without corrupting data.

At that point, you have two choices—and both hurt.

You start with raw IndexedDB (or a thin wrapper around it). Pretty quickly, you realize IndexedDB isn't a relational database. Want to join two tables? You’re writing manual JavaScript loops and merging cursors in memory. Want a compound filter with sorting and pagination? You’re fighting key ranges and writing dozens of lines of imperative code for what should have been a 3-line query.

Frustrated with IndexedDB, you reach for SQLite WASM or PGlite. Now you have real relational queries, which feels great—until you look at the trade-offs:

After hitting this wall one too many times while building offline-capable apps, I asked a simple question: What if we built a relational database engine natively for the browser from scratch?

Today, I’m really excited to launch WebDB.

Desktop databases need a SQL text parser because queries come over a network socket as raw strings. In the browser, your application code and your database live in the exact same runtime. Why are we serializing objects into strings just to parse them back again?

Because WebDB compiles fluent TypeScript AST directly into compact binary opcodes (OP_INDEX_SCAN, OP_RESULT_ROW, etc.), we don't need to bundle a massive C string parser.

The result? A full relational engine—with B+Tree indexes, joins, aggregates, subqueries, and crash-proof ACID transactions—inside a ~19 KB gzipped WebAssembly core (~51 KB raw), with a pure JS fallback included.

No SQL strings to escape. You get full TypeScript autocompletion for schemas, composite B+Tree indexes, JOINs, GROUP BY, HAVING, and aggregates:

If you ever want to see what the cost-based query planner is doing under the hood, just call .explain() on any query to inspect the generated VDBE bytecode instructions directly.

One of the most annoying parts of offline apps is wiring manual event buses around database writes so your UI knows when to re-render.

WebDB ships with isolated framework subpaths (under 1 KB gzipped each) that automatically inspect your query AST—including JOINs and subqueries. When a relevant table mutates in the current tab, a Web Worker, or another open browser tab (via BroadcastChannel), your UI updates automatically:

Because WebDB compiles TypeScript directly into binary opcodes and avoids C parser overhead, both the ~19 KB WASM engine and even the pure JS fallback beat official SQLite WASM (:memory:) across common relational workloads (tested on a MacBook Pro M1 Max):

Don't just take my numbers for it—you can run the live benchmark suite on your own machine here.

To make debugging local databases easier, I also built the WebDB Studio Playground.

Right in your browser, you can write queries with full autocompletion, inspect raw binary 4 KB slotted pages in real time, visualize B+Tree structures, and even share live compressed .webdb.gz databases via URL.

WebDB is completely open-source under the MIT license. If you’ve ever felt the friction of building offline-first or local-first web apps, I’d love for you to try it out, break it, and let me know what you think!

What's been your biggest headache when dealing with client-side storage in the browser? Let me know in the comments!

#9781. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

Note: This article contains affiliate links, meaning we make a small commission if you buy any premium plan from our link.

#9780. 5 Common Prescription Drugs Linked To Memory Loss

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Memory loss is not always a result of ageing.

Here are five types of drugs that can affect memory.

The older type of antidepressants — known as tricyclics — have been linked to memory loss.

Around half of people taking them report problems concentrating and one-third say they have memory loss.

Benzodiazepines include drugs marketed under the names Valium, Ativan, Klonopin and Xanax.

These drugs are often prescribed for anxiety and other mental health issues such as OCD, insomnia and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Unfortunately they are also linked to memory loss and even Alzheimer’s.

Dr Helene Alphonso, a psychiatrist and Director of Osteopathic Medical Education at Texas University, said:

“Current research is extremely clear and physicians need to partner with their patients to move them into therapies, like [modern] anti-depressants, that are proven to be safer and more effective.”

Statins are prescribed to many people to keep their cholesterol in a safer range.

The Food and Drug Administration lists memory loss, forgetfulness and confusion as possible side-effects of the drug.

Some people do report memory problems when taking them, but the studies conducted so far are inconclusive.

Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and are used to lower blood pressure.

They are also prescribed to those with congestive heart problems.

Beta-blockers, though, may also cause the loss of emotional memories.

They have even been tested as a way of treating post-traumatic stress disorder because of their ability to block emotional memories.

Again, though, the studies are not conclusive.

People who cannot sleep are sometimes prescribed so-called ‘Z-drugs’.

The ‘Z-drugs’ have been linked to memory loss: especially losing the ability to make new memories.

They have also been reported to cause strange behaviours like driving or cooking with absolutely no memory of the event.

Where possible consider a psychological therapy or applicable alternative to using these drugs.

Naturally, you should always consult your physician before making changes to your medication.

#9779. Why SSH Still Matters After More Than 30 Years

Imagine managing a server located thousands of miles away. You need to update its software, investigate an application failure, or change a configuration file. You cannot physically access the machine, but you still need to work with it almost as if it were sitting on your desk.

Today, this is a completely ordinary task. Engineers connect to remote servers, execute commands, transfer files, and maintain infrastructure from practically anywhere in the world. Much of this is possible because of a technology called SSH, or Secure Shell.

SSH is one of those technologies that most people outside the IT industry have probably never heard of, even though it plays an important role in the systems they use every day. Websites, banking platforms, cloud applications, and enterprise services all depend on infrastructure that is frequently managed through SSH.

What makes SSH particularly interesting is its longevity. The protocol was introduced in 1995, when the internet was a very different place. Yet, more than three decades later, SSH remains an essential tool for software developers, system administrators, DevOps engineers, and security professionals.

To understand why it has survived for so long, it is worth looking at the problem it was originally designed to solve, how its security mechanisms work, and how its role has changed as computing has evolved.

At its simplest, SSH is a network protocol that allows two computers to communicate securely over a potentially untrusted network. The most familiar use case is remote terminal access. A user opens a terminal, connects to another computer, and begins executing commands.

This command asks the SSH client to connect to a remote machine at the specified IP address using the username admin. If authentication succeeds, the user can work with the remote system through a command-line session. But SSH is much more than a remote terminal protocol. It can also transfer files, execute individual commands, carry application traffic through encrypted tunnels, and provide secure authentication for automated processes.

The importance of SSH comes from three fundamental security properties:

Confidentiality means that network traffic is encrypted so that someone intercepting the communication cannot easily read its contents.

Integrity means that the receiving system can detect unauthorized changes to transmitted data. An attacker should not be able to modify commands or responses without the modification being detected.

Authentication helps establish that the client is communicating with the intended server and that the user attempting to access the server has appropriate credentials.

These properties work together. Encryption alone would not be enough if an attacker could impersonate the destination server. Similarly, verifying a user's identity would provide limited protection if commands and passwords were transmitted openly.

One of the most interesting aspects of SSH is how much happens before the user sees a command prompt. Typing a simple SSH command starts a sequence involving network communication, cryptographic negotiation, identity verification, session-key generation, and user authentication. Understanding these steps helps explain why SSH is considered secure and where configuration mistakes can introduce risks.

SSH normally operates over TCP, using port 22 by default. The client first establishes a TCP connection with the server. TCP provides a reliable communication stream, ensuring that data is delivered in order and that lost segments can be retransmitted.

At this point, the connection itself is not yet protected by SSH encryption. The client and server then exchange protocol identification strings, which indicate the SSH protocol versions and software implementations they support. A server might identify itself with a string similar to:

This tells the client that the server implements SSH protocol version 2. The version exchange is followed by negotiation of the cryptographic algorithms that will be used during the session.

SSH does not depend on a single encryption algorithm. Instead, the client and server each advertise supported algorithms and select compatible choices. These choices include algorithms for key exchange, server authentication, symmetric encryption, and message integrity.

Modern SSH implementations may use algorithms such as:

These algorithms serve different purposes.

For instance, public-key cryptography helps authenticate identities and establish cryptographic secrets, while symmetric cryptography handles the continuous flow of data after the session has been established.

This distinction is important because asymmetric cryptographic operations are generally more computationally expensive than symmetric encryption. Rather than encrypting every terminal command with a public key, SSH uses key exchange to establish session secrets and then employs efficient symmetric encryption for the actual communication.

The next challenge is creating encryption keys that both computers can use without exposing those keys to observers on the network. Traditionally, SSH has accomplished this through mechanisms such as Diffie-Hellman or elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

The basic principle is that the client and server exchange mathematical values that allow them to calculate a common secret independently. The secret itself is not transmitted directly. An attacker who captures the publicly exchanged values should not be able to reconstruct that secret under the security assumptions of the selected algorithm. SSH then uses the agreed secret, together with other values from the handshake, to derive cryptographic keys for the session.

Modern algorithms can also provide forward secrecy. Forward secrecy means that obtaining a server's long-term private key at a later date should not, by itself, allow an attacker to decrypt previously recorded sessions. This matters because attackers sometimes store encrypted network traffic in the hope of decrypting it in the future.

However, secure key exchange alone does not prove that the client is connected to the correct server. That requires a separate authentication mechanism.

Every properly configured SSH server has a host identity represented by one or more cryptographic key pairs. During key exchange, the server uses its host private key to sign information associated with the handshake. The client verifies the signature using the server's public host key. This demonstrates that the server possesses the corresponding private key, but another question remains: is this public key really associated with the intended server?

SSH clients commonly maintain a file called known_hosts, usually located inside the user's .ssh directory. When connecting to a server for the first time, the client may display the server's host-key fingerprint and ask whether to trust it. After the key is accepted, it is stored for future comparisons.

On subsequent connections, the client checks whether the presented host key matches the previously trusted identity. If the key changes unexpectedly, the client can display a prominent security warning.

This mechanism helps protect against man-in-the-middle attacks, where an attacker attempts to impersonate the destination server. There is one important limitation: accepting an unknown host key without verifying its fingerprint can establish trust in the wrong machine. Organizations can reduce this risk by distributing verified host keys or using SSH host certificates.

Once the secure transport has been established and the server's identity has been checked, SSH authenticates the user. SSH supports several authentication methods, including passwords, public-key authentication, and additional mechanisms configured by the server.

Public-key authentication is especially common in professional environments. To use it, a user generates a key pair consisting of a public key and a private key.

The public key can be installed on a server, commonly in the user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file.

The private key remains on the user's device and should be protected from unauthorized access.

During authentication, the client uses the private key to create a digital signature over session-specific authentication data. The server verifies that signature using the corresponding public key and checks whether that identity is authorized. If the verification succeeds and the server's authentication policy is satisfied, access is granted.

The important point is that the private key is never sent to the server. The client proves possession of the private key by producing a valid signature. This makes public-key authentication particularly useful for automated systems, because it avoids repeatedly transmitting reusable passwords.

However, the private key still needs protection. If it is stolen and is not sufficiently protected, an attacker may be able to impersonate the user.

After successful authentication, the client can request a terminal session, execute a command, open a file-transfer subsystem, or establish another supported connection channel. For an interactive terminal, the server normally starts the user's shell or another configured command. From this point onward, terminal input and output travel through the SSH encrypted transport.

When the user types a command, the client packages the data into SSH messages, encrypts and authenticates them, and transmits them to the server. The server checks the integrity of the incoming data, decrypts it, and passes the relevant content to the destination process.

Responses travel back using the same general mechanism in the opposite direction, with separate cryptographic keys and state. A network observer can usually still identify the participating IP addresses, connection timing, and approximate traffic volume. However, with properly configured modern algorithms, the observer cannot read the commands or responses.

SSH can also periodically perform a new key exchange during an existing session, a process called rekeying. This limits the amount of traffic protected under a single set of session keys.

Although SSH often appears to be a single protocol, SSH-2 is organized into three major layers.

The transport layer establishes secure communication. It handles cryptographic negotiation, server authentication, encryption, integrity protection, and key exchange.

Above it, the user authentication layer determines whether the connecting client is authorized to access the requested account or service.

Finally, the connection layer manages the actual activities taking place inside the secure transport.

One particularly useful feature of the connection layer is multiplexing. SSH can carry multiple logical channels over a single encrypted connection. For example, a single SSH transport may carry an interactive terminal while also supporting forwarded TCP connections or other permitted channels.

This separation makes SSH much more flexible than a protocol designed only for remote command execution. The same security foundation can support several different kinds of applications without each application having to implement its own encryption and authentication mechanisms.

SSH has become an essential technology across modern IT infrastructure. Although it was originally developed for secure remote access, it now supports a wide range of activities, from software development to infrastructure automation.

Server and Cloud Infrastructure Management

SSH allows engineers and system administrators to securely access remote servers, execute commands, troubleshoot problems, and manage systems hosted in cloud platforms such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud.

Software Development and Git Repositories

Developers use SSH to securely interact with Git repositories hosted on platforms such as GitHub and GitLab. It enables authentication using cryptographic keys, making everyday operations like cloning repositories, pushing code, and pulling updates more convenient and secure.

SSH is widely used in automated deployment and configuration management. Tools such as Ansible rely on SSH to execute commands, install software, and manage large numbers of servers without requiring manual intervention.

Protocols and tools such as SFTP and SCP use SSH to securely transfer files between computers. They are commonly used for backups, application deployments, and exchanging sensitive information between systems.

SSH can create encrypted tunnels that allow applications to communicate securely with remote services. This is particularly useful for accessing databases, internal applications, and other resources that are not directly exposed to the internet.

Network administrators use SSH to configure and maintain routers, switches, firewalls, and other networking devices. It is also widely supported by embedded Linux systems, including Raspberry Pi devices.

SSH is sometimes confused with other security technologies, particularly HTTPS and VPNs. All three can protect network communication, but they serve different purposes.

HTTPS is primarily designed to secure communication between clients and web services using HTTP over TLS. It is the technology that protects ordinary web browsing and many web APIs.

A VPN creates a protected connection that can carry traffic for a wider range of network applications, depending on its design and configuration. It is often used to provide remote access to private networks or to connect separate networks.

SSH, by contrast, is primarily designed around secure remote access, authenticated sessions, command execution, file transfer, and application tunneling.

For example, a software engineer might use HTTPS to access a monitoring dashboard, a VPN to reach an organization's internal network, and SSH to investigate a particular Linux server. These technologies are not necessarily alternatives. They are often used together. An SSH session may run through a VPN, while the server being administered hosts applications that communicate with users over HTTPS. Understanding their different responsibilities is important when designing secure infrastructure.

SSH has an excellent reputation, but it is not a universal solution to every security problem.

One of its limitations is that encryption protects data during transmission, not necessarily after it reaches its destination. If the remote server has already been compromised, an encrypted SSH connection does not prevent an attacker controlling that server from observing commands or accessing data available to the session. Similarly, if a user's private key or workstation is compromised, an attacker may be able to initiate legitimate-looking SSH connections.

SSH also does not automatically provide detailed accountability for every action taken during a session. A server may log the fact that a user authenticated, but reconstructing every interactive command and its effects may require additional auditing or session-recording mechanisms.

There are operational limitations as well. Managing SSH access across a handful of servers is relatively straightforward. Managing it across tens of thousands of servers, contractors, automated workloads, and changing cloud environments is considerably more difficult. Organizations need reliable processes for granting access, revoking credentials, controlling privileges, and monitoring unusual activity.

This is why SSH increasingly operates alongside identity-management systems, access gateways, configuration-management platforms, and security-monitoring tools. Its cryptographic design remains important, but maintaining the security of the surrounding environment is equally essential.

It is easy to overlook foundational technologies because they become part of everyday routines. For an experienced engineer, opening an SSH session may take only a few seconds. The command is familiar, the connection is established, and attention immediately shifts to the task on the remote machine. Yet behind that ordinary interaction is an enormous amount of engineering. The client and server negotiate compatible algorithms, establish cryptographic secrets, verify identities, authenticate the user, and maintain an encrypted communication channel. All of this happens with very little visible complexity.

SSH also demonstrates an important principle in software architecture: well-designed technologies can remain useful long after the environments in which they were created have changed. When SSH first appeared, cloud computing did not exist in its modern form. Containers, Kubernetes, GitHub, and today's automated deployment platforms were still years away.

Nevertheless, the fundamental need for secure communication between computers remained the same. The protocol was designed around that need rather than around one particular product or infrastructure model. As a result, SSH could be adapted to new environments without losing its core purpose.

Today, it connects developers to cloud servers, supports automated operations, secures file transfers, enables controlled access to internal services, and helps administrators manage critical systems. It is not always visible to end users, and it is rarely the technology that attracts attention during major software announcements. But when a production system fails or an engineer needs access to a remote machine, SSH is often one of the first tools they reach for.

SSH started with a relatively simple problem: how to access a remote computer without exposing sensitive information to anyone who could observe the network. Its solution became much more than a secure replacement for Telnet.

Over the following decades, SSH evolved into a versatile protocol supporting remote administration, authentication, file transfers, tunneling, automation, and large-scale infrastructure operations. Its lasting importance comes from the combination of security, flexibility, interoperability, and practical usefulness.

At the same time, SSH reminds us that strong cryptography does not remove the need for proper system administration. Key management, access control, endpoint security, and regular maintenance remain critical to protecting the systems that depend on it.

More than 30 years after its introduction, SSH continues to serve as a trusted foundation for secure remote access. And as infrastructure becomes increasingly distributed, automated, and interconnected, that fundamental capability is unlikely to become less important.

#9777. Why Your Next IDE Might Actually Be a Git Client

A few weeks ago I wrote about why I left GitKraken and built Gitoryx. That post was about the tool I left behind. This one is about something I noticed while building the replacement: the more I used Gitoryx day to day, the less I opened my IDE for anything other than editing code.

That's not a small shift. For years, the IDE was the center of gravity. Everything else, the terminal, the Git GUI, the AI assistant, orbited around it as a separate window you alt-tabbed into. I didn't plan to change that. It just stopped making sense once the pieces lived in one place.

I used to run three windows to get anything done: an IDE, a terminal, and a Git GUI. Sometimes a fourth for a chat-based AI tool. Every time I wanted to check what a command actually did to my working tree, or verify that a build I'd just kicked off hadn't broken something, I'd switch windows, refocus, and try to remember what I was looking for in the first place.

None of that felt slow in the moment. It felt normal, the same way GitKraken's lag felt normal until I noticed it. But normal isn't the same as necessary. Gitoryx ships with an integrated terminal built on xterm.js and a real PTY, so running a command and looking at the resulting diff happen in the same window, one click apart instead of one window swap apart.

The honest reason this matters isn't that switching windows takes long. It's that switching windows breaks your attention, and attention is the thing you actually run out of during a long coding session. Fewer context switches throughout your day add up to more hours where you're actually thinking about the problem instead of hunting for the window that has the answer.

Here's where the terminal-in-the-Git-client setup earns its keep the most: when an AI coding assistant is actively working in your repo.

I run AI tools in the terminal a lot now, the same way most developers do. The problem was never running them. The problem was watching what they did. In a separate terminal app, checking the AI's progress means alt-tabbing out of my Git client, watching a wall of text scroll by, then alt-tabbing back to see what actually changed in the code. By the time I got back to the diff view, I'd usually forgotten exactly which part of the output I was trying to correlate with which file.

With the terminal built into the same app as the commit graph and diff viewer, I can run the AI session in one pane and watch the working tree update in real time in the other. If it touches a file I didn't expect, I see it the moment it happens, not five minutes later when I finally switch back. That's not a hypothetical convenience. It's the difference between catching an unwanted change immediately and finding it after three more commits have piled on top of it.

I've caught more than one AI-generated change that touched a file outside the scope of what I'd asked for, simply because the diff was sitting right next to the terminal output instead of a full window away. Nothing dramatic, usually a formatting pass that spread further than intended, but it's the kind of thing you only catch if you're actually watching, and you only watch consistently if watching is easy. It's also changed how I think about commits themselves when an agent is doing the typing: they stop being a record of what I wrote and become checkpoints I use to keep control of what something else wrote, a shift I go into in more detail in Vibe Coding With Git.

There's a habit spreading through teams that I think deserves more scrutiny than it's getting: letting AI write the commit message and hitting commit without reading it.

I get why it happens. Writing a good commit message takes a few seconds of thought, and when you're deep in a flow state, those seconds feel like friction. But a commit message isn't decoration. It's the thing a teammate reads six months from now to understand why a change was made, or the thing you read yourself during a git bisect session at 11 PM trying to find out which commit broke production. When that message is generated and never reviewed, you get technically accurate but generic text that describes what changed without ever explaining why, and a Git history that slowly stops being useful as a record of decisions.

Gitoryx has AI commit messages built into the commit panel, supporting Anthropic Claude, OpenAI, GitHub Models, or a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint if you're running something local. But the feature only works the way I intended if you treat it as a first draft, not a final answer. The AI reads your staged changes and proposes a title and description. You still see it in the same panel where you'd write it by hand, and you still edit it before it goes anywhere. Nothing commits itself.

That distinction matters more than it sounds like it should. A commit-message generator bolted onto a separate tool, outside your Git client, makes it easy to copy-paste and move on without a second look. One that lives inside the same panel where you're already reviewing your diff puts the proposed message right next to the actual change, so editing it before committing is the path of least resistance instead of an extra step you skip when you're tired.

I want to be careful here, because I'm not arguing the IDE is going away. Editing code, real editing with syntax awareness, refactoring tools, and language server support, still needs a dedicated environment, and nothing about a Git client replaces that.

What I am arguing is narrower and, I think, more interesting: the IDE's claim to being the single hub where a developer spends their day is weakening. A few years ago, the IDE was where you edited code, ran your terminal, checked your Git status through a thin sidebar panel, and increasingly, chatted with an AI assistant bolted on as a plugin. Each of those secondary functions was there because there wasn't a better place for it, not because the IDE was the natural home for version control or command execution.

Now that Git clients are picking up real terminals and real AI integration, that default is getting questioned. A Git client that shows you your full history, lets you run commands without leaving the window, and helps you write the record of what you did and why, starts to look less like a viewer for git log and more like a second hub competing for the center of your workflow, doing the specific job an editor's built-in Git panel was never built to do (a distinction I laid out in Why Desktop Git Clients Still Matter). I don't think it fully displaces the IDE. I think it starts splitting the day: the IDE for writing and shaping code, the Git client for everything around understanding, verifying, and recording that code's history.

If that split keeps deepening, in a few years the tool you open first each morning, the one you keep in the primary window while everything else is secondary, might not be your IDE at all. It might be your Git client.

None of this required a chat-based AI assistant living inside a Git client, and I want to be precise about that, because it's tempting to describe a bigger product than what actually exists. Gitoryx doesn't have a conversational AI or an AI code reviewer. What it has is an integrated terminal so you can run whatever AI tooling you already use without leaving the app, and an AI commit message feature that proposes text you review before it becomes permanent history. Both are modest on their own. Together, in the same window, they change how much attention switching your day requires.

That's the actual argument. Not that AI belongs everywhere, but that when it does show up in your workflow, having it inside the tool that already shows you your code's real state, instead of scattered across a separate terminal, a separate chat window, and a separate Git GUI, keeps you closer to what's actually happening and keeps you the one making the final call.

If the story in my first post was about leaving a tool that had stopped serving me, this one is about what I built to replace it starting to serve a bigger role than I expected. I didn't set out to make a case against the IDE. I just kept noticing I needed it less.

Try Gitoryx free. It's free forever for public repos, native on macOS and Windows, and the integrated terminal and AI commit messages are both available on the free plan.

#9774. How to explain a crypto product on video without sounding like a pitch

Crypto and web3 products have a trust problem before they have a feature problem. The viewer has seen the rocket emojis and the "100x" claims, so the first question is not "what does it do?" but "is this a scam?" A product video that ignores that question loses people in the first ten seconds. Here is how I plan these videos when a wallet, protocol or exchange team asks me to animate something.

Skip the hype opener. Open on the specific job the product does for a specific person: "move funds between chains without three separate apps" or "see exactly what a contract will do before you sign it." A plain, checkable sentence signals that nothing here depends on excitement.

People trust what they can follow. The strongest web3 videos I have worked on spend most of their time on one real flow on screen:

If the product has a fee, show it on screen at the moment it applies. Hiding a fee in a footer is the fastest way to confirm the viewer's suspicion.

Terms like gas, bridge, staking or liquidity are familiar to your core users and invisible to everyone else. Instead of a glossary, give each term a small visual the first time it appears (a fuel gauge for gas, two ledgers linked by an arrow for a bridge) and then use the word normally. Experts are not slowed down, and newcomers are not lost.

Anything that sounds like a return, a guarantee or advice needs review by someone who knows your jurisdiction's rules before it goes into a script. A safe default is to describe what the product does and show the risks plainly, not to describe what the user will earn. A video that states a limitation clearly usually builds more trust than one that avoids every limitation.

Real UI beats stylised renders. If the interface is changing every sprint, build the video from layered screen captures so a changed button is a quick replacement instead of a full redo. Keep the voice-over script in a separate file for the same reason.

The landing page and the first step of onboarding are where this kind of video does the most work. A cut-down 15 to 20 second version with captions works for social, since most viewers will watch it muted.

I keep a short page on how I approach this kind of video here: https://vaghelabhavesh.com/services/web3-crypto-product-video.html

#9771. Run a Game Studio for $0/Month: My Complete Free Tool Stack (Engine, Art, Video, Marketing)

Posted on Nov 6 • Originally published at open.substack.com

Quick math for you: engine license, art software, video editing suite, hosting. The "standard" indie stack costs somewhere between $50 and $100 every month before you've sold a single copy of anything.

I built my entire studio workflow on a stack that costs exactly zero. Not free trials. Not crippled versions. Five tools that take you from blank screen to published game — and marketed. Here they are.

1. GDevelop — The No-Code Engine That Doesn't Fight You GDevelop is an open-source, no-code game engine that runs in your browser or as a desktop app. No C#, no C++, no missing-semicolon debugging sessions at 2 AM.

The event system reads like plain English: "If the player presses the right arrow key, move the player to the right." You spend your brain cycles on game design, not syntax.

The underrated killer feature: one-click exporting. Android, HTML5 web, Windows/Mac/Linux desktop — same project. When you're a solo dev, removing porting friction is the difference between shipping on three platforms and shipping on none.

2. Inkscape — Vector Art Without the Adobe Tax Free, open-source vector editor. The important word is vector: unlike raster images, vector art scales infinitely. Your character sprites, icons, and UI stay razor-sharp on a phone screen and on a 4K monitor alike — same asset, zero pixelation.

For 2D game assets specifically, this beats paying a monthly Illustrator subscription for functionality that Inkscape covers.

3. OBS Studio — The Recording Standard Modern game dev means building a brand alongside the game: devlogs, tutorials, trailers. OBS Studio is open-source, rock-solid, and the de facto industry standard for capture and streaming.

Set your resolution and frame rate once, then forget it exists. One-button recording when you want simple; multi-scene, multi-track audio setups when you don't.

The long-game detail I love: if you ever pay for the Studio version, your project timelines transfer perfectly. No relearning, no lost work. The tool grows with your studio instead of trapping you.

5. Dev.to — Your Zero-Maintenance Traffic Engine Not software — a platform. Building and maintaining your own site costs time and money; posting your devlogs and tutorials on dev.to gets you in front of an enormous existing developer audience for free.

Embed your YouTube videos directly into posts, pick good tags, and let dev.to's internal traffic and SEO do the discovery work for you. Free backlinks, organic growth, zero servers to manage.

The Stack at a Glance Engine GDevelop $0 2D art Inkscape $0 Screen capture OBS Studio $0 Video editing DaVinci Resolve $0 Marketing/audience dev.to $0 Total $0/month

The barrier to entry for game development has never been lower. The most important variable isn't your tool budget — it's your consistency. This stack removes every excuse except sitting down and building.

What's in your free stack? Anything I'm missing? Drop it in the comments 👇
