#9653. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9652. New book explores how Ukraine’s artists are shaping the memory of war

Cover illustration by Kyiv-based Ukrainian artist Sergiy Maidukov

As the war grinds on in Ukraine, almost five years after Russia’s full-scale invasion, The Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins reminds us in her timely and sobering new book how artists and writers register the human cost of the conflict.

“The argument of this book is that the literature and art made by these people, some of whom have lost their lives, will shape the war’s memory,” Higgins boldly asserts. Artists, writers, poets and filmmakers are her vital and sympathetic touchstones across cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv and Lviv.

“When a friend, the defence and security editor of The Guardian, suggested I might think about going to Ukraine, I agreed immediately that it was a good idea,” she writes. “I said it lightly, impulsively, and without realising that going there would change me.”

This odyssey begins in the autumn of 2022, encompassing three years of reporting trips to Ukraine. The arc of the narrative is epic and emotional, from arriving in Kyiv on a bright, beautiful day (10 October) to a final documentary account of the destruction of Bakhmut in the east, where an elderly lady called Nina surveys streets blitzed by shell holes that “were once perfectly ordinary”.

Along the way, Higgins deftly interweaves personal milestones such as slowly grasping the Ukrainian language—who knew “verbs of motion” could be so onerous?—detailing how “the war leaked into every [language] lesson”. Dealing with the anger felt by Ukrainians facing “the outrage of violence” is another test for the author, who anchors her account by observing the impact of Ukrainian art and artists, both historic and contemporary.

As testament to the violence and destruction, Higgins draws on a film by the Kharkiv artists Daniil Revkovskyi and Andrii Rachynskyi shown in the Ukrainian pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale. Civilians. Invasion (2023) is an hour-long collage of unedited videos found online that mirror the true reality of constant bombs and bullets.

Higgins’s survey of artists is essential as a journal of record, bringing to the fore figures such as Marharyta Polovinko, whose macabre, penetrating drawings of roaming monsters can be set, Higgins argues, alongside the work of Spanish artist Francisco Goya—famed for The Disasters of War (1810-20)—or the First World War and Weimar imagery of the German painter Otto Dix. Immortalising these creative figures, who may go unnoticed outside Ukraine, is a significant commemorative act (Polovinko was killed in action in 2025, aged 31).

A trained classicist, Higgins frames the events and trauma of the war through Greek mythology. She likens the character of Cassandra—who was condemned to prophesy only the truth but never be believed—to “resolute Ukrainian women, eloquent and truth-telling”, neatly segueing into one of Ukraine’s greatest works of literature, a seminal poem written by Lesya Ukrainka around 1907 (Cassandra: A Dramatic Poem).

Victoria Amelina, a Ukrainian novelist and war crimes investigator who died aged 37 in July 2023 from severe injuries sustained during a Russian missile strike, is one of these “Pale Cassandras”. Amelina was instrumental in bringing to light the buried journal of the late writer Volodymyr Vakulenko who documented life under occupation.

In commemorating friends and colleagues like Amelina, Higgins is searing and eloquent. “[…] grief leaked out of me,” she says, “and I felt like a vessel with no shape, porous, lacking capacity to hold anything.” Such frank admissions could jar but in shaping a war’s memory, this narrative benefits from such measured, personal interludes.

Cultural erasure is a weapon of war: at least 120 Ukrainian museums have been damaged in the conflict, according to the country’s culture ministry. Russian president Vladimir Putin is not only attempting to annihilate the military and political leadership, but also its cultural warriors in a ruthless bid to vanquish the existence of a sovereign Ukraine. Higgins’s book is a bulwark against this campaign; as a personal memoir it is deeply affecting, and as a journalistic record it is transformative.

• Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, by Charlotte Higgins, published by Jonathan Cape, 272pp, £22 (hb), 20 August

#9650. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

A 16-year-old adolescent presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of vomiting, tactile fevers, and a mild headache that went away 2 days earlier. The patient denies any abdominal or flank pain, dysuria, diarrhea, or other complaints. When specifically questioned, she acknowledges a slight cough but has no shortness of breath or chest pain.

The patient’s vital signs are normal except for an elevated temperature (100.3 °F) and a pulse rate 133 beats per minute. Initial physical examination is otherwise normal with no rash, tonsillar exudate, rales, murmur, flank tenderness, or other abnormality. Chest radiographs (Figure 1-2) and blood work are ordered. Laboratory results are within normal range except for an elevated white blood cell count (19,000/μL). Pregnancy and COVID-19 PCR tests are negative.

#9644. New book charts American artist’s lifelong devotion to the South Seas

Robert Lee Eskridge’s Stone-Fishing (around 1930) shows the Polynesian fishing practice of using ropes and stones Courtesy of www.GalleryHawaiiana.com

This is a book about a love affair, one that ran so deep it yielded thousands of watercolours, hundreds of oil paintings and three illustrated books. The painter Robert Lee Eskridge (1891-1975) first visited the South Seas in May 1927, when his ship pulled into the harbour of Papeete, Tahiti. Seeking respite from the grey skies and bone-chilling winters of Chicago, he was instantly smitten and kept returning to the South Seas, eventually making his home in Honolulu, Hawai’i.

Little in Eskridge’s early life had predicted that infatuation. Born in Philadelphia, he attended the Art Institute of Chicago, studied in Paris with the Cubist painter André Lhote, and travelled across Europe for three years. His style, fusing Art Deco patterns with a form of relaxed realism, won him gigs as an illustrator and artist, culminating in a high-profile commission to produce murals for the lobby of the newly rebuilt Palmer House hotel in Chicago. On the eve of his departure for Tahiti, he chose Marco Polo as his subject. (The murals were painted over in 1966.)

Falling in love with the South Seas is not a unique experience. Names like Herman Melville, Robert Louis Stevenson and Paul Gauguin conjure lush tropical forests, foam-crested waves lapping pristine beaches, and carefree Islanders performing hula dances: a vision inevitably darkened by the damages wrought by colonialism. The Islanders Eskridge painted, unlike Gauguin’s, are not immobilised by the artist’s desire to project meaning into them. They are walking, working, dancing, fishing and making music, living fully in the present even as they honour their rich traditions.

Eskridge’s enthusiasm for Islander culture finds a perfect match in biographer Cook’s enthusiasm for Eskridge. While the more lyrically effusive passages in this volume might not appeal to everyone, the lavish illustrations drawn from multiple collections and the excellent captions help us understand the breadth, range and sophistication of a supremely adaptable painter who deserves to be better known. (Regrettably, some images—of the lost Chicago murals, for example—are AI-produced).

Eskridge’s paintings, whether they show bustling street scenes or re-create rituals he witnessed, vibrate with life. As a young man, he was entranced with Sandro Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (around 1485, in the Uffizi Gallery), and that painting’s revelatory spirit lingers on in Eskridge’s bright, luminous colours or in the way he arranges groups of people around a central figure or an activity.

His training under Lhote shapes the cascading abstract forms Eskridge uses in the background of works such as Stone Fishing (around 1930, Gallery Hawaiiana). In this ancient Polynesian fishing practice, men use ropes with stones to herd leaping fish into shallower waters—a communal effort as well as an occasion for individual daring, represented here beautifully by the young man in the middle, who jumps to grab a fish from the air. A later masterpiece is Hilo Wharf (around 1949, Honolulu Museum of Art), a harbour scene, in which Eskridge blends shirtless workers and the bodies of gigantic tuna fish, some already packed up, into an intense drama of shapes, colour and movement.

Since Eskridge treated the Islanders and their culture with respect, they accepted him as one of their own, Cook tells us. They even asked Eskridge to represent them at the Chicago World’s Fair in 1933. Invitations followed to provide Hawaiian-themed murals for the McCoy Pavilion in Honolulu’s Ala Moana Park and, later, to design clothes for the Hawai’ian label Paradise Sportswear.

Always one to defy expectations, Eskridge, at age 64, married Helen Gebhardt and settled in Olympia, Washington. But the Islands kept calling. He died in April 1975 at a hotel in Honolulu named, appropriately, Hale-kulani, “house befitting heaven”.

• C.J. Cook, Robert Lee Eskridge, South Pacific Dreams Publishing, 344pp, 509 col. illust., $59.95 (hb), published 11 August

• Christoph Irmscher is a critic and biographer

#9633. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9631. Underappreciated artists from the Chelsea Hotel are finally getting their due

Bettina standing outside of the Chelsea Hotel, New York Courtesy the artist’s estate

Since its opening in 1884, New York’s Hotel Chelsea has been famed as a hotbed of creativity—a seedy yet alluring beacon drawing artists, musicians and bohemians of all kinds. While the luminaries associated with the place (Mark Twain, Janis Joplin, Andy Warhol) are well known, less famous residents are only now beginning to gain recognition.

Among the more recently “discovered” artists who once called the Chelsea home are the late Bettina (1927-2021), Ching Ho Cheng (1946-89), Bernard Childs (1910-85), Herbert Gentry (1919-2003), Nicola L. (1932-2018) and Teruko Yokoi (1924-2020). Many of their relatives still live in the building; some feel their presence to this day.

“It’s happened many times, Ching contacting me,” Cheng’s sister, Sybao Cheng-Wilson, tells The Art Newspaper. She moved into the Chelsea in the 1980s to take care of her brother, who was dying of Aids. For years after Cheng’s death, the bathroom light bulb would flicker on his birthday, 26 December; Cheng-Wilson became convinced it was his way of checking in on her.

For her part, Cheng-Wilson became dedicated to preserving her brother’s legacy. She held onto both his art and the apartment where he made it. She even raised her daughter at the Chelsea, despite its notorious reputation as a hedonistic haven.

Judith Childs and her artist husband moved into the Chelsea in 1966. “My parents were a little horrified by the whole building,” she recalls. “It was not an elegant hotel.” Childs still lives in the first-floor apartment she and Bernard once shared, surrounded by his soft-hued geometric abstractions that seem to glow from within.

Bernard Childs’s work at the Armory Show 2026 Courtesy Bank

In September, these works—imbued with an almost cosmic fluidity—were the subject of a solo stand at New York’s Armory Show with the Shanghai- and New York-based gallery Bank. The 1970s canvases—priced between $14,000 and $55,000—stood out amid the more than 200 exhibitors at the fair; they hung above a fuzzy, cantaloupe-coloured carpet that enhanced the works’ warm, luminous quality.

Showing an essentially forgotten artist like Childs was a bit of a risk for Bank founder Mathieu Borysevicz. “He’s been off the map for so long,” says the gallerist, who just began working with Childs’s estate. The artist’s work was featured in Documenta in 1959; that same year, he had a solo show at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. But Childs’s previous dealer, Jason McCoy Gallery, last gave the artist an in-person solo show in 2013; the gallery itself closed in 2024.

Borysevicz already had experience helping artists from the storied hotel emerge from the shadows, having worked with the Cheng estate since 2021.

Over Cheng’s short but prolific career, the artist developed four major bodies of work, beginning with psychedelic paintings inspired by Tibetan spiritualism before experimenting with airbrushed gouache, graphite on torn paper and rusted surfaces made using iron and copper oxide on paper. The artist, who appeared in last year’s Sixties Surreal at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art, will have his first major retrospective in September 2027 at the Addison Gallery of American Art in Andover, Massachusetts.

Ching Ho Cheng in his Chelsea Hotel studio in 1985 Courtesy the artist’s estate

Cheng had moved into the Chelsea in 1976, where he befriended Childs. Judith and Cheng-Wilson have stayed close over the years, united by their shared devotion to preserving and promoting their late loved ones’ work. It was Cheng-Wilson who introduced Judith to Borysevicz.

Another friend of Childs, from his time in Paris in the 1950s, was Herbert Gentry—an African American painter known for his jazz-inspired abstractions. He arrived at the hotel in the late 1960s; Gentry’s second wife, the artist Mary Anne Rose, joined him in 1978. She still lives at the Chelsea and now oversees his estate.

“Herbert’s work is so distinctive stylistically, but he was also foundational in bridging what was happening in North America and Europe,” says Gentry’s dealer, Jeffrey Lee of the New York gallery Ryan Lee. By December, the artist will have work simultaneously in museum group shows in Alabama, Germany and Martinique, plus a solo show at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts, Sweden.

But not all Hotel Chelsea artists have family members on the premises to safeguard their legacies. When the reclusive Bettina died in 2021, management quickly began clearing out her apartment. The unit was nearly bursting with the conceptual artist’s life’s work, to the point where Bettina slept in a lawn chair in the hallway, as memorably captured in the 2022 documentary Dreaming Walls: Inside the Chelsea Hotel. That would have been the end of the story had Bettina not connected with the Moroccan artist Yto Barrada in her final years.

Barrada fervently believed in the value of Bettina’s work, and its need to be saved from the dumpsters and shared with the world. Before Bettina’s death, Barrada presented the older artist’s sculptures at the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council Arts Center on Governors Island, leading to an appearance in Greater New York 2021 at MoMA PS1. When Bettina died, it was Barrada who saved the contents of her apartment from the trash. The estate, which Barrada oversees with the assistance of Anna McCormick-Goodhart, is now represented by Ulrik in New York; a solo show at the Ruth Foundation for the Arts in Milwaukee closed in April.

One of Bettina’s index cards outlining the details of her unrealised exhibition The Chelsea Hotel: Artists at Work Courtesy the artist’s estate

“There is a lot to sort and sift through, and it leaves wonderful traces of the history of the making of her works, of her travels, of the people in her life—it’s very densely layered,” McCormick-Goodhart says.

In her later years, Bettina—whose work encompasses photography, printmaking, painting, sculpture, textile and commercial design—was known largely for her eccentricities. But she also planned an ambitious, albeit unrealised, exhibition to show her neighbours’ art. A series of typed index cards from the 1980s reveal the artist list and potential venues for The Chelsea Hotel: Artists at Work. The exhibition would have featured the works of Cheng, Childs, Gentry and Rose, among other residents.

Another artist in this heady milieu was Nicola L. A documentary film-maker, who turned her own lens on her home of nearly 30 years for the 2014 film Doors Ajar at the Chelsea Hotel, Nicola L. is best known for her “functional sculptures”—anthropomorphic furniture shaped like a massive foot, the silhouette of a head and other body parts. In a critique of the objectification of women’s bodies, some mimic the female form, but they somehow avoid feeling overly sexualised.

Nicola L. was largely overlooked until London’s Tate Modern included her work in a broader view of international Pop art for its 2015 exhibition The World Goes Pop. Nicola L.’s first institutional solo show took place in 2017 at New York’s SculptureCenter; the London gallery Alison Jacques began representing her estate after the artist’s death in 2018. A retrospective, When the Earth Turned the Other Way, closed earlier this month at Belgium’s Museum of Contemporary Art in Antwerp, and the travelling museum show I Am the Last Woman Object wrapped up a European tour in March.

Installation view of Nicola L.: When the Earth Turned the Other Way, Museum of Contemporary Art, Antwerp, Belgium Courtesy Alison Jacques

Nicola L. was the catalyst behind the Chelsea Hotel residents’ successful fight to keep their apartments after new ownership embarked on an 11-year renovation project to transform the property into a high-end hotel—where rates start at around $500 per night. It was at her urging that the residents banded together to successfully protect their rent-stabilised tenancy.

“The Chelsea was a safe haven for these artists,” says Christophe Lanzenberg, Nicola L.’s son. “The Chelsea allowed them to thrive and stay in New York, instead of getting kicked out of places where rents were coming up.”

Today, there are 42 families still living at the Chelsea. (One artist, Gerald DeCock, is facing eviction at the end of February after 31 years in residence.) Over the years, those remaining have forged tight bonds.

When Childs died, Gentry sent Rose downstairs to keep Judith company. Rose and Nicola L. shared a Long Island City studio for years. As Nicola L.’s health began to decline due to Alzheimer’s, Rose and Judith kept a close watch. They let her sons know when their mother could no longer live alone.

Though its heyday as a refuge for free-spirited artists is long past, the hotel is still deeply connected to its creative history, including artists who checked out decades ago. The lobby, stairwells and hallways are filled with works of art, some said to have been given to the longtime manager Stanley Bard (1934-2017) in lieu of rent. A new Japanese restaurant, Teruko, opened in the basement last year featuring paintings by its namesake, Teruko Yokoi (1924-2020), who lived at the Chelsea from 1957 to 1960, during her marriage to Sam Francis (1923-94).

Teruko Yokoi’s Untitled (1959) will be on offer on Hollis Taggart’s stand at New York’s ADAA Fair in November Courtesy Hollis Taggart

“I was a baby when she was just coming out of art school, juggling having a newborn and continuing to paint. Her studio was actually in the apartment,” says Yokoi’s daughter, Kayo Malik, who is also a custodian of her estate. But when the couple hosted parties for friends like Mark Rothko and Al Leslie, Francis would have Yokoi put her paintings away, hiding her work.

At the Teruko restaurant, the artist’s pieces are displayed in the dining room, enjoyed and appreciated by guests gathering to share a meal—“a full circle moment”, Malik says. The artist is also the subject of a solo show, Seasons, at New York’s Hollis Taggart (until 25 November). And the gallery is bringing one of Yokoi’s Hotel Chelsea-era works, Untitled (1959), to the ADAA Fair at New York’s Park Avenue Armory (12-16 November); there, it will be on offer at a two-person presentation with the artist Michael West (1908-91). Meanwhile in Los Angeles, the artist has a solo show currently on view at James Fuentes Gallery (until 7 November).

Yokoi eventually moved to Switzerland after separating from Francis. Determined to show her work, she opened two dedicated museums in her native Japan, enjoying a long career across three continents. But Malik still feels close ties to her first home at the Chelsea, that formative chapter in Yokoi’s life, and its vibrant artist community.

“The hotel has had an incredible life,” Malik says.

The influence of New York on the Greek-born artist informs an exhibition designed to fill in the gaps of her story

The five-gallery fair was staged inside one of Manhattan's most famous hotels

The artist’s former residence opens a restaurant named Teruko this month, featuring her works

#9630. Does β‑Blocker Use Increase Depression Risk?

The association between β-blocker use and depression was investigated in a population-based observational study recently published in the journal Drug Safety.

While depression is often cited as an adverse effect of β-blocker use, there is limited evidence supporting this causal relationship. To better understand the association between beta blockers and the risk of new-onset depression, the study authors analyzed data from the UK population-based Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) GOLD database.

“We identifed patients aged 18-80 years with an incident depression diagnosis between 2000 and 2016, and matched controls, and estimated the risk (odds ratio [OR]) of depression in association with use of β-blockers,” the study authors explained.

Findings of the analysis revealed an increased risk of developing depression among short-term users of β-blockers compared with no use at all (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.91; 95% CI, 1.72-2.12).

Among short-term users, increased risk of depression was mainly restricted to patients with a neuropsychiatric disorder taking propranolol (aOR 6.33, 95% CI 5.16–7.76).  Patients on propranolol for a cardiovascular indication were found to be at slightly elevated risk of depression (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14–1.82). Apart from propranolol, no other lipophilic β-blocker or hydrophilic β-blocker was found to increase the risk of depression.

Additionally, no association was observed between long-term use of β-blockers and the risk of depression (aOR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.85-0.94).

“Our findings suggest that the reported association between use of β-blockers and depression may not be causal but rather a result of protopathic bias,” the study authors concluded.

Bornand D, Reinau D, Jick SS, Meier CR. β‑blockers and the risk of depression: A matched case–control study. Drug Safety. Published online January 19, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-021-01140-5.

#9620. Edward Hopper biography, Kvareli Foundation in Georgia, Marisa Merz in Turin—podcast

Edward Hopper: A Life by Louis Shadwick (2026), featuring Edward Hopper's (Self-Portrait) (around 1925–30)

From breaking news and insider insights to exhibitions and events around the world, the team at The Art Newspaper picks apart the art world’s big stories with the help of special guests. An award-winning podcast hosted by Ben Luke.

As a biography of Edward Hopper is published, containing a wealth of new material, Ben Luke speaks to its author Louis Shadwick about his quest to find the truth behind the artist that he writes “has become more myth than man in the popular imagination”.

Edward Hopper's Old Ice Pond at Nyack (around 1898-1900)

Copyright 2026, Heirs of Josephine N. Hopper/Licensed by DACS, London

In Georgia, the Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, a new private museum, opens this weekend. The Art Newspaper’s digital editor, Alexander Morrison, speaks to Nino Sulkhanishvili, the creative director, about it.

An aerial view of the the Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, in the countryside around 150km east of the Tbilisi

And this episode’s Work of the Week is E il naufragar m’è dolce in questo mare (1980) by Marisa Merz. This installation is the centrepiece of an exhibition at the Castello di Rivoli in Turin, one of three presentations in the Italian city marking the 100th anniversary of Merz’s birth. Ben talks to the co-curator of the Castello di Rivoli show, Marianna Vecellio.

Marisa Merz's E il naufragar m’è dolce in questo mare (and to be shipwrecked is sweet to me in this sea), 1980

Plus, a horror show in London and a Flemish masterpiece in Bruges

What’s behind the troubles facing auction houses and galleries? Plus, Sasha Skochilenko recounts her experience of being arrested—and incarcerated—in Russia, and the story behind a 1937 Surrealist painting by Ernst

Plus, a protest-themed tenth edition of the Performa Biennial and a restored portrait by Hans Holbein the Younger
